questions.enonce_markdown: How is nominal national income different from real national income? (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** National income is the value of the goods and services produced in an economy (or the incomes earned by its residents) during a year. It can be measured in two ways, which give different pictures of economic change.

**1. Nominal national income**

- National income measured at **current prices**, that is, at the prices ruling in the year of measurement.
- It can rise because **output has increased**, or simply because **prices have risen** (inflation), so a rise does not necessarily mean that more goods and services are produced.
- It is also called national income at current prices or money national income.

**2. Real national income**

- National income **adjusted for changes in the price level**, that is, measured at **constant prices** (the prices of a base year).
- It is obtained by deflating the nominal figure:

$$
\text{Real national income} = \frac{\text{Nominal national income}}{\text{Price index}} \times 100
$$

- It shows the change in the actual **quantity** of goods and services, so it is the appropriate measure of changes in output and economic growth.

**3. Hypothetical example**

Suppose nominal national income rises from 10 000 billion FCFA in year 1 (price index 100) to 11 000 billion FCFA in year 2 (price index 108). Nominal income has risen by 10%, but real income in year 2 is $\frac{11\,000}{108} \times 100 \approx 10\,185$ billion FCFA in year-1 prices, a rise of only about 1.9%. Most of the apparent increase was due to higher prices.

**Conclusion.** Nominal national income is measured at current prices and is affected by inflation; real national income is adjusted for price changes and measures the true change in output.

questions.enonce_markdown: Does a rise in real national income per head provide the only suitable indicator of improvement in living standards? (15 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Real national income per head (real income divided by the population) is the most widely used indicator of living standards, because it adjusts for price changes and for the number of people who share the income. It is useful, but it is **not the only suitable indicator**, and taken alone it can be misleading.

**1. Why real national income per head is a useful indicator**

- It adjusts for **inflation** (real) and for **population growth** (per head), so it shows the average quantity of goods and services available per person.
- It is **easy to calculate and compare** over time and between countries, and is usually correlated with health, education and consumption.

**2. Hypothetical illustration of its limits**

Real national income may rise while real income per head falls. Suppose real income is 10 000 billion FCFA in year 1 with a population of 20 million, so income per head is 500 000 FCFA. In year 2 real income rises to about 10 185 billion FCFA but the population rises to 20.6 million: income per head is about 494 000 FCFA, a **fall** (this is only an example). A rise in real national income per head is therefore needed, but not sufficient.

**3. Limitations of real income per head as the only indicator**

1. **Distribution of income.** It is an *average*; it says nothing about how income is shared. If the gains go to a small rich group, most people may be no better off. Measures such as the Gini coefficient or the share of the poorest 20% give this information.
2. **Non-marketed output and the informal economy.** Subsistence farming, household work, voluntary work and underground (informal) activities are excluded or poorly measured, which is important in developing economies such as Cameroon, so living standards are underestimated (or distorted when output moves from the household to the market).
3. **Composition of output.** A rise may come from military spending, investment goods or the repair of damage, which do not improve consumption; and the *quality* of goods (better health care, technology) is poorly captured.
4. **Leisure and working conditions.** Income may rise because people work longer hours or in worse conditions; a gain in leisure time improves welfare but is not counted.
5. **Environmental damage and depletion of resources.** Pollution, deforestation or oil depletion are not subtracted, and the cost of cleaning up may even be added, so income may rise while the quality of life falls.
6. **Social and non-economic aspects.** Health, life expectancy, literacy and education, freedom, security, housing, access to clean water and electricity, and political stability are important to well-being but are not measured by income.
7. **Prices and exchange rates in international comparisons.** Converting incomes at market exchange rates ignores differences in the cost of living between countries; purchasing power parity (PPP) adjustments are needed.
8. **Externalities and public goods.** Social costs and the benefits of public services such as roads and schools are only partly reflected.

**4. Other indicators**

- The **Human Development Index (HDI)**, combining income per head, life expectancy and education.
- **Social indicators**: life expectancy, infant mortality, literacy, school enrolment, doctors or hospital beds per 1 000 people, access to safe water and electricity.
- **Distribution indicators**: the Gini coefficient, the percentage of the population below the poverty line.
- **Environmental and happiness indices**, and measures of economic welfare that adjust national income for leisure, pollution and non-marketed work.

**Evaluation.** Real national income per head is a good *starting point*, and the different indicators usually move together in the long run, so it is a reasonable summary in the absence of better data. But because of the problems of distribution, measurement, quality of life and sustainability, it should be **supplemented** by social and distributional indicators; an accurate view of changes in living standards needs a set of indicators.

**Conclusion.** No, a rise in real national income per head is not the only suitable indicator of an improvement in living standards, because it ignores income distribution, non-marketed output, leisure, the environment and social aspects such as health and education; it should be used together with other indicators such as the HDI.
